title: Latency Optimization
summary: Reducing end-to-end and tail latency in request-driven systems: why p50 hides the experience that matters, how fan-out compounds tail latency, and why queueing makes latency explode long before a system is 'full.'

slides.markdown:
Every prior topic in this group has been about making *something* faster. This one is about which number you're actually trying to move — and the honest answer is almost never the average.

Latency optimization is dominated by two facts that surprise engineers new to it: the tail (p99, p99.9) is usually what users feel, not the mean; and once a resource gets busy enough, latency doesn't creep up gently — it explodes, non-linearly, well before the resource looks "full" on a utilization graph.

Get those two ideas and the rest of this topic — fan-out, critical paths, capacity vs. reducing work — is really about applying them to real request-response systems.

slides.sectionTitle: Average latency hides the real experience
slides.subTitle: Why p50 isn't the number that matters
slides.markdown:
The average (mean) latency is dominated by the bulk of requests, which is exactly why it's the wrong number to optimize for user experience. Consider 1,000 requests where 990 take 50ms and 10 take 5,000ms. The mean is about 99.5ms — looks fine. But 1% of your users waited 100x longer than everyone else, and the mean doesn't hint at that at all.

The median (p50) has almost the same blind spot: it tells you what the *typical* request experiences, but a typical user makes many requests over a session, and each one is a fresh roll of the dice against the full distribution — including the tail. A user who makes 20 requests in a session has a real chance of hitting at least one p99-or-worse request, even though any single request is "probably fine."

This is why performance work reports and targets **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99, sometimes p99.9) rather than the mean: they describe the shape of the experience across the whole user base, not just its center. A system is not fast because its average is fast — it's fast because its tail is short.

slides.sectionTitle: Tail latency and why it compounds
slides.subTitle: p99 and p99.9 across a fan-out
slides.markdown:
**p99** means 1% of requests are slower than this value; **p99.9** means 1 in 1,000 are. These sound like edge cases you can ignore — they aren't, because of how they compound.

If a single call has a 1% chance of hitting its p99-or-worse latency, and your request depends on **10 independent calls** to return before you can respond, the chance that *at least one* of them is slow is roughly 1 − (0.99)^10 ≈ **9.6%** — not 1%. Your overall p99 is set by the worst of ten dice rolls, not by any individual call's own p99. This is sometimes called the "tail at scale" problem (the term comes from Google's influential paper on the topic).

The practical consequence: the more dependencies a request fan out to, the worse its overall tail gets, even if every individual dependency has an excellent tail latency in isolation. Reducing fan-out, or making the system tolerant of one slow dependency (timeouts, hedged requests — covered later in this topic), matters more as a system grows more service-oriented, not less.

Picture a request fanning out to ten downstream calls in parallel, all of which must return before the response is assembled. Each call individually has a clean, tight latency distribution with a p99 barely above its p50. But because the overall response waits on the *slowest* of the ten, the overall p99 is visibly worse than any single call's own p99 — the diagram should show nine fast bars finishing early and one long bar (a different one each time, in practice) dragging the total out.

This is the concrete picture behind the "tail at scale" math in §3: parallel fan-out doesn't make you as fast as your fastest call, or even as your typical call — it makes you as slow as your slowest call, and which call that is varies request to request as different dependencies have their unlucky moment.

slides.subTitle: What's actually blocking the response
slides.markdown:
The **critical path** is the sequence of operations that must complete, in order, before the response can be sent — anything not on it can be slow without affecting overall latency at all. Two calls that run concurrently and both must finish are both on the critical path; a call whose result isn't needed until after the response is sent (e.g., fire-and-forget analytics logging) is not on it, no matter how slow it is.

Finding the critical path requires understanding the actual dependency graph of a request, not just listing everything it touches. A request that makes five downstream calls but only genuinely depends on the slowest two of them — say, an auth check and a database read that must both complete, while three other calls are for optional, best-effort enrichment — has a critical path of two calls, not five. Optimizing one of the other three does nothing for latency; it might improve something else (completeness of the response) but not speed.

A distributed trace (mentioned in Profiling Techniques) is the practical tool for seeing this: it shows which spans overlap in parallel versus which are strictly sequential, making the true critical path visible instead of assumed from the code's call structure.

slides.sectionTitle: The three levers for reducing latency
slides.subTitle: Caching, parallelizing, precomputation
slides.markdown:
Once you know the critical path, three levers actually shorten it:

- **Caching.** If a value on the critical path is read far more often than it changes, serve it from a fast in-memory or nearby cache instead of recomputing or re-fetching it. This is the single highest-leverage latency fix available when applicable, because it can remove an entire dependency's latency from the critical path outright.
- **Parallelizing independent calls.** If two calls on the critical path don't depend on each other's results, run them concurrently instead of sequentially — the critical path becomes the *slower* of the two, not their sum. A request doing an auth check then a database read sequentially at 20ms + 30ms becomes 30ms total if they don't actually depend on each other.
- **Precomputation.** If a value is expensive to compute but doesn't depend on the specific request (e.g., a recommendation list refreshed every 5 minutes rather than computed live per request), compute it ahead of time on a schedule and just serve the precomputed result on the critical path.

All three share a pattern: they move work either off the critical path entirely (precomputation, caching) or off its sequential sum (parallelizing). None of them make the underlying work itself faster — they change *when* or *how often* it happens relative to the request.

slides.subTitle: Latency explodes as utilization approaches 100%
slides.markdown:
Basic queueing theory (the M/M/1 model, the simplest case) gives a shape every performance engineer should recognize: expected wait time scales roughly with **ρ / (1 − ρ)**, where ρ (rho) is utilization — the fraction of capacity actually in use. At 50% utilization, that factor is 1. At 80%, it's 4. At 90%, it's 9. At 95%, it's 19. At 99%, it's 99.

The curve is not linear — it's a hyperbola that goes vertical as utilization approaches 100%. This is why a system running at 92% CPU can have dramatically worse latency than one at 75%, even though "92% busy" sounds only modestly worse than "75% busy" — the queueing cost, not the raw utilization number, is what you actually feel.

The practical consequence: capacity planning that targets "keep utilization under 70-80%" isn't conservative padding, it's respecting where the curve starts turning vertical. Running a system at 95% sustained utilization to save on infrastructure cost is trading a large, compounding latency cost for a linear cost saving — almost never a good trade for anything latency-sensitive.

slides.sectionTitle: Adding capacity vs reducing work per request
slides.markdown:
| | Adding capacity | Reducing work per request |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | More servers/cores/replicas to lower utilization ρ | Making each request itself cheaper (caching, algorithmic fix, fewer calls) |
| **Effect on queueing** | Directly lowers ρ, which per §7 has an outsized effect on tail latency near saturation | Lowers total work, which can lower ρ indirectly if throughput is unchanged, or raise throughput at the same ρ |
| **Cost** | Scales with infrastructure spend, often close to linear | One-time engineering cost, then close to free at runtime |
| **Speed to deploy** | Fast — often minutes (autoscaling) | Slow — requires design, implementation, testing |
| **Ceiling** | Bounded by budget and, eventually, Amdahl's Law if the bottleneck is a serial resource | Bounded by how much real waste exists to remove |

Both levers lower ρ, which is why they're not actually in opposition — a mature system uses capacity as the fast, temporary response to a latency spike (autoscale now) while treating a genuine algorithmic or architectural fix as the durable one (reduce the work so you need less capacity going forward). Relying on capacity alone forever is treating a queueing symptom without ever fixing what's driving demand.

slides.sectionTitle: Chasing average latency, breaking the tail
slides.markdown:
A team adds a cache to speed up the common case, and the dashboard's average latency drops nicely. Three weeks later, p99 complaints roll in — the cache-miss path got slower, because the caching layer added overhead (a lookup, a possible network hop to a cache service) that every request pays, while only cache *hits* get the benefit. Cache hits (say, 95% of traffic) got much faster; cache misses (the 5% that were probably already slower, being less common/less cached data) got slower still. The average improved because it's dominated by the 95%; the tail got worse because it's dominated by the 5%.

This pattern repeats anywhere an optimization helps the common case at a fixed cost to every request: a fast-path check added to every request to skip expensive validation for well-formed input speeds up the 99% of requests that are well-formed, while the 1% that fail the check now pay for both the check *and* the original expensive path.

The fix is measuring the change against percentiles, not just the mean, before calling it a win — and specifically checking whether the improvement's cost (however small per-request) is being paid by requests that were already in the tail.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level tail-latency technique
slides.markdown:
Once you accept that tail latency compounds across fan-out (§3), one direct countermeasure is a **hedged request**: if a call hasn't returned within, say, its p95 latency, fire a second identical request (possibly to a different replica) and take whichever comes back first, cancelling the other. This trades a small amount of extra load (most hedges never fire, since most requests are fast) for a large cut in tail latency, because the odds that *both* the original and the hedge are unlucky are far lower than the odds either one alone is.

The trade-off is real: hedging adds load to the system precisely when parts of it are already slow, which can worsen the situation under genuine overload rather than a one-off unlucky request — so hedging is typically capped (hedge at most X% of requests) and paired with backpressure so it doesn't turn a localized slowdown into a self-inflicted overload.

A closely related technique is aggressive **cancellation**: once a response no longer needs a particular downstream call's result (say, the fastest of several redundant replicas already answered), actively cancel the others rather than letting them run to completion and waste resources — this keeps hedging's extra load bounded and short-lived instead of compounding.

Two downstream calls that don't depend on each other, done sequentially versus concurrently:

```python
# Sequential: critical path = sum of both calls
async def get_dashboard_sequential(user_id):
    profile = await fetch_profile(user_id)     # ~30ms
    recent = await fetch_recent_orders(user_id) # ~40ms
    return combine(profile, recent)              # critical path ~70ms

# Parallel: critical path = the slower of the two
async def get_dashboard_parallel(user_id):
    profile_task = fetch_profile(user_id)
    recent_task = fetch_recent_orders(user_id)
    profile, recent = await asyncio.gather(profile_task, recent_task)
    return combine(profile, recent)              # critical path ~40ms
```

The only change is *when* each call starts — both versions do exactly the same total work, but the parallel version's critical path is the max of the two calls (§5) instead of their sum. This is often the highest-return, lowest-risk latency fix available: no new infrastructure, no caching invalidation to reason about, just confirming the two calls genuinely don't depend on each other's output before running them concurrently.

The complete approach: measure and report percentiles, not the mean (§2), understand why tail latency gets worse as fan-out grows (§3, §4), find the actual critical path rather than assuming it from the code (§5), and apply the three levers — caching, parallelizing, precomputation (§6, §11) — to shorten it. Watch utilization against the queueing curve, not just as a raw percentage (§7), and treat capacity and work-reduction as complementary, not either/or (§8). For genuinely tail-latency-sensitive paths, hedging and cancellation are the advanced technique once the basics are in place (§10). And always re-check a win against the tail, not just the average, before calling it done (§9).

The next two topics — Memory & GC Performance and Concurrency Performance — are where two of the most common causes of tail latency spikes actually live: a GC pause and lock contention are both, mechanically, a request getting stuck in a queue it can't see.
